items.quote: mettalls are of no use in Physick, at least in the civill life
items.name: any who out of their simplicity shall say
items.note: A view the author reports in order to answer it: some say metals are of no use in physick. He calls it said out of simplicity.

items.quote: there is no agreement or likenesse especially of those perfect Mettalls with mans body
items.name: any who out of their simplicity shall say
items.note: Second part of the reported view: the perfect metals have no likeness with man's body. Reported to be rejected.

items.quote: created, though not for Mans food yet for his Physick
items.note: The author holds that metals, fruit of the Elements like living things and vegetables, were created for man's physick, not for his food.

items.quote: man partaketh of those Three first
items.note: The text names 'those Three first' as one known set that man partakes of; the lines given do not list them here.

items.quote: the Animall, Vegetable and Minerall sperm or seed have but one rise or originall, and differ onely in Quality of Place and Receptacle
items.note: The author's answer: the seed of animals, vegetables and minerals has one origin; the difference lies only in place and receptacle.

items.quote: See Theophrast. his Manuel.
items.name: Theophrast. his Manuel
items.note: The margin note names a writing beside the passage on metals in physick.

items.quote: since Man hath Physick for his body from the world because he is a world, therefore all Mineralls are for Mans good
items.note: The note gives the ground: man is a world and has his physick from the world, so all minerals are for his good. Whether these are the author's words or drawn from the writing named is not shown.

items.quote: that which is contained in the Physicall body is applyed to his minerall
items.note: The note speaks of man's 'minerall', as if man has a mineral part to which what is in the physical body is applied.

items.quote: Animall, Vegetable, and Minerall principles are one and the same in all things, but have various Receptacles
items.note: The three kinds of principles are said to be the same in all things; only the receptacles differ.

items.quote: which is the generall seed of all things or subject of the first matter
items.note: The text says what the 'one most principall and generall principall kind' is: the general seed of all things, or subject of the first matter.

items.quote: to be distributed into three principall kinds, Animall Vegetable, and Minerall
items.what: three principall kinds, Animall Vegetable, and Minerall
items.note: The one general kind is set out as divided into three named kinds.

items.quote: from which Nature hath the nature of Quick-silver to create every other Compound
items.note: Quick-silver is named here as a 'nature' that Nature has from the general kind and by which every compound is made, not as one metal among others. The lines given do not explain further.

items.quote: All things are from one Principle, and tendeth to one
items.note: The author states that all things come from one principle and tend to one.

items.quote: In Orpheus his Night and Hippocrates his river Orcus all things are but One
items.name: Orpheus; Hippocrates
items.note: Two named figures are brought as saying the same: in Orpheus's Night and Hippocrates's river Orcus all is one.

items.quote: like Anaxagoras his Pamsperm, which Aristotle unjustly condemned
items.name: Anaxagoras
items.note: Anaxagoras's Pamsperm is likened to these; the author says Aristotle condemned it unjustly, and (after the note mark) 'because he did not well understand it'. The margin note N176 at this place is an unread gap of foreign script.

items.quote: that one onely Nature the Essence and Matter of all things came forth upon the Stage of this world, by the pleasure of God, which Nature is the Specifick of every Creature
items.note: The one Nature is called the essence and matter of all things and the 'Specifick' of every creature.

items.quote: various wonderfull bodies and of manifold distinction according to the disposition and variety of the Place and Receptacle, and according to the agitation and operation of the Universall spirit
items.note: The differences between bodies are laid to two things: the place and receptacle, and the working of the Universal spirit.

items.quote: This is the set Order for the government of the sublunary Family, that Mineralls should nourish Vegetables, Vegetables feed beasts, and beasts men
items.what: the set Order for the government of the sublunary Family
items.note: The text names an order of nourishment: minerals feed vegetables, vegetables beasts, beasts men.

items.quote: which could not be if the nature of one thing did not by affinity partake of the nature of another
items.note: The author argues from this order: one kind could not nourish another unless their natures were akin and shared in the first kind.

items.quote: Thus also the Spirit of life is united through out the whole body of man, but is various according to parts of the body in which it is.
items.note: The note compares the one Nature in different receptacles with the one Spirit of life that differs by the part of man's body it is in.

items.quote: All things flow from one Fountaine, which after they have done their work and quitted the Stage of Vanity, are returned to their own places
items.note: All things come from one fountain and return to their own places after their work, where the text says they have unchangeable rest.

items.quote: That universall Spirit which liveth in and quickneth this whole Masse, which worketh all in all, and filleth the whole world; that Power of God, which comprehendeth all the world in it
items.what: That universall Spirit; that Power of God
items.note: The text sets apart one thing under two names, the universal Spirit and the Power of God, and then gives what others call it.

items.quote: Agrippa calleth it the subject of all mirability, the Ens or Being that cannot be comprehended by sence
items.name: Agrippa
items.note: Agrippa's name for the universal Spirit, as the text gives it.

items.quote: Avicen saith, it is the Soule of the world powred into all things, building on the authority of Plato, the Arabians and Caldeans
items.name: Avicen
items.note: Avicen's name for it, the Soul of the world; the text adds on whose authority he builds.

items.quote: this we must hearken to without any superstition or Idolatrous worship, giving honour onely to One God
items.note: The author limits how the teaching of a world soul is to be taken: without superstition or worship, the honour to God alone.

items.quote: Rom. 8.
items.name: Rom. 8
items.note: The margin note names a writing beside the passage on all things returning to rest.

items.quote: See Paracelsus his Apocalyps of Herines.
items.name: Paracelsus his Apocalyps of Herines
items.note: The margin note names a writing of Paracelsus beside the passage on the universal Spirit.

items.quote: The Soule of the world is a kind of united life, filling, gathering and knitting together all things
items.note: The note says what the Soul of the world is: a united life that fills and knits all things together. Words after this in the note have unread letters.

items.quote: by infusing into them occult qualities which are commonly called the Fift Effences
items.note: The note says the Soul of the world makes things fruitful by putting occult qualities into them, and gives the common name of these qualities.

items.quote: is the invisible Fire or fiery vigour by which all things are
items.note: The note says what Nature is: the invisible fire or fiery vigour by which all things are multiplied (the words before it call Nature an image; one letter there is unread).

items.quote: Nature many times makes it selfe merry with its magistery or mastership and rejoyceth in its master
items.note: The note pairs 'magistery' with 'mastership' as one sense, and speaks of Nature making merry with it.

items.quote: Nature, I say, is that medium which by an Harmonicall consent joyneth the lowest things to the highest
items.note: The author says in his own person what Nature is: the medium that joins lowest to highest. Other accounts of Nature stand at N178 and CH3.40.

items.quote: sometimes is called Animall, sometimes Vegetable, sometimes Minerall, according to the diversity of the subject or receptacle
items.note: The one Nature takes the three names from the subject or receptacle it is in.

items.quote: in the three Families of Nature
items.note: The three kinds are named together as the three Families of Nature.

items.quote: that Silesiac child in our age, which was born though not with a golden yet with a gilded tooth in the left and lower jaw, which I did both see and handle
items.note: The author gives as an example of Nature's working a child born with a gilded tooth, which he says he saw and handled himself at Prague.

items.quote: those who diligently seek out the Hermetick Phylosophy and the marvellous works of God
items.note: The text names a philosophy and the group who seek it; to them the example is said not to be strange.

items.quote: it is not unlawfull to pry into those things which exceed even naturall order
items.note: The author holds that inquiry into things beyond natural order is lawful.

items.quote: these are not so much astonyed at the sports of Nature
items.note: The gilded tooth and the like are named 'sports of Nature'.

items.quote: from the intimacy of more hid and secret Phylosophy they know that that same Spirit and minerall Nature which produceth Gold in the bowells of the Earth is also in Man
items.note: The text says a more hidden and secret philosophy holds this knowledge: the spirit and mineral nature that makes gold in the earth is also in man.

items.quote: That Spirit in Gold is the same with the generating spirit of all Creatures, and is the same and onely generative Nature diffused through all things
items.note: The spirit in gold is identified with the one generating spirit of all creatures.

items.quote: This Spirit now hath assumed a Naturall body
items.note: The spirit is said to have taken a natural body; the lines given do not say which body.

items.quote: It is that which first moveth and ruleth Nature in all naturall things, it preserveth all things
items.note: This spirit is said to be the first mover and ruler of Nature and the preserver of all things.

items.quote: Albertus Magnus writeth, that in his time there hath been Gold found in the bodyes and heads of some that were hanged
items.name: Albertus Magnus
items.note: A report given to Albertus Magnus: gold found in the bodies and heads of the hanged.

items.quote: There is not, saith he, that thing Elementated of the four Elements in which Gold Naturally may not be found in the last subtiliation thereof
items.name: Albertus Magnus
items.note: Words given to Albertus from 'his Book of Mineralls': gold may be found in every thing made of the four elements, at its last subtiliation.

items.quote: the Phylosophers say that the matter of their Mystery may be had every where, because it consisteth in every Elementated thing
items.name: the Phylosophers
items.note: A saying given to 'the Phylosophers': the matter of their Mystery is to be had everywhere. The text gives the reason, that it is in every elementated thing.

items.quote: the greatest Minerall vertue is in every Man, but especially in the head among the teeth
items.name: Albertus
items.note: Given to Albertus: the greatest mineral virtue is in every man, chiefly among the teeth; he reports gold grains found among the teeth of the long buried.

items.quote: which could not be if there were not a minerall vertue in Man, which minerall vertue is in the Elixer of Phylosophers
items.note: The mineral virtue in man is said to be the one in the Elixer of Phylosophers. The sentence does not show whether this conclusion is Albertus's or the author's.

items.quote: In his Mineralls.
items.name: Albertus
items.note: The margin note names the writing of Albertus that the passage draws on.

items.quote: Morienes that excellent Phylosopher, the most skilfull and expert Chymiologer
items.note: The text introduces Morienes with the name 'Chymiologer'.

items.quote: when he answered King Calid who inquired after the matter of the Elixer; It is of thee O King, said he
items.name: Morienes
items.note: Morienes's answer to King Calid on the matter of the Elixer: it is of the king himself.

items.quote: and thou are in its Mine
items.name: Morienes
items.note: The rest of Morienes's answer: the king is in the mine of the matter. 'Mine' is used of a man.

items.quote: he saith that he got his matter out of a mean and worthlesse thing
items.name: Raymund Lully
items.note: Given to Raymund Lully: his matter came out of a mean and worthless thing. The thing is not named.

items.quote: Wherein he never a jot differed from Raymund Lully that fearcher into this Magistery
items.note: The author holds that Morienes and Lully say the same; the work is here called 'this Magistery'.

items.quote: Lullius was a divine & most compleat Phylosopher, whom Paracel. blamed without a cause.
items.note: The note praises Lullius and says Paracelsus blamed him without cause.

items.quote: whom Paracel. blamed without a cause
items.note: Here Paracelsus is said to have blamed a complete philosopher wrongly; in CH3.40 he is said to have 'the absolute knowledge of all Divine and Humane sciences'.

items.quote: The matter of a stone is said to be in every thing in respect of the first
items.note: The note says in what respect the saying 'in every thing' is meant: in respect of the first mover in natural things (one letter of that word is unread).

items.quote: which is calld the Vegetall Spirit, by whom our matter of a stone goeth beyond the rest
items.note: The first mover in natural things is given its name, the Vegetall Spirit; by it 'our matter of a stone' is said to exceed the rest. The note adds that this spirit is in animals and vegetables as well as minerals.

items.quote: Remember that Man is the most noble Creature of all, in whom there is the Naturall Mercuriality of the four Elements
items.name: Riplaeus à Portis
items.note: Given to Riplaeus à Portis, whom the author says agrees with both: in man is the natural Mercuriality of the four elements.

items.quote: which is of little worth, and may be got out of its Mine by art
items.name: Riplaeus à Portis
items.note: Still Riplaeus's words: this Mercuriality is of little worth and can be got out of its mine by art. No step is given.

items.quote: in every thing there is every thing potentially, though it doth not actually appear
items.name: Rhasis
items.note: Given to Rhasis, 'In his Book of Divinity': every thing is in every thing potentially. The author says Rhasis does not altogether dissent from Riplaeus.

items.quote: I forbear to cite more Authors, though I might produce a great heap of Phylosophers, who confirme these things
items.note: The author stops citing and claims many more philosophers confirm the same.

items.quote: not by common and outside arguments, but by solyd reasons drawn from the inside of things
items.note: He sets reasons drawn from the inside of things against common, outside arguments.

items.quote: But these things are by the by.
items.note: The author marks what went before as an aside from his main matter.

items.quote: The Chymicall way of Subtiliating Extracting, and Separating being imperfect, was not much used in Galens dayes
items.note: The author says the chymical way was imperfect and little used in Galen's days, and adds that it was altogether unknown to Galen.

items.quote: for they knew not how to separate the bark and husk from the kernell
items.note: The work of separating is spoken of as parting bark and husk from kernel; the section heading uses 'bark and rind' of the true physick.

items.quote: he tryed all wayes and means to distinguish the facultyes of simple medicines, and discern the hot parts of vineger from the cold
items.name: Galen
items.note: Galen's own words as reported: he tried every way to tell apart the faculties of simple medicines and the hot and cold parts of vinegar.

items.quote: to separate the contrary parts of vineger as well as of milk
items.note: The step Galen is said to have sought a device for: separating the contrary parts of vinegar, as is done with milk. No method is given.

items.quote: who in this thing might have obtained his desire if he had been well skild in the Distillatory Art
items.note: The author holds that the Distillatory Art would have given Galen what he sought.

items.quote: Nor is it any disgrace to Hippocrates or Galen that they knew not these things
items.note: The author does not blame Hippocrates or Galen for not knowing these things.

items.quote: which is the order and series of Gods works, and obey the power, word and command of God, and borroweth all its vertue and efficacy from him
items.note: The text says in a parenthesis what Nature is: the order and series of God's works, with all its virtue borrowed from him. Other accounts of Nature stand at CH3.32 and N178.

items.quote: they doe not bestow upon mankind all things together and at once, but doe communicate particular gifts to severall ages
items.note: God and Nature give particular gifts to particular ages and persons, not all at once.

items.quote: if Galen had lived when Paracelsus did, he would not have envyed, but reverenced his learning, nor would he have been ashamed of his Coals
items.note: The author's claim about Galen: he would have revered Paracelsus's learning and not been ashamed of the coals.

items.quote: to know how to separate the three first (qualities) in vineger
items.note: A bracketed word explains 'the three first' as 'qualities' here; N181 speaks of 'the three first things' and CH3.28 of 'those Three first'.

items.quote: to learn the preparations of those high Magisteryes and Elixirs
items.note: The text names a class of preparations as the higher thing to be learned.

items.quote: neither would he have refufed to blow the coals or temper his stuffe, or watch his work
items.note: Three tasks of the work are named: blowing the coals, tempering the stuff, watching the work.

items.quote: Colerick and Melancolick Philerastian Physitians, who have not learned so much as their A. B. C. in the Spagyrick Physick
items.note: The author says the opposing physicians have not learned the first letters of the Spagyrick Physick.

items.quote: the Creation and composition of the internall Astrall Man, much lesse of the Mechanick Spirits of diseases
items.what: the internall Astrall Man; the Mechanick Spirits of diseases
items.note: Two things are named as matters these physicians know nothing of; the lines given do not explain them.

items.quote: that never sufficiently commended Paracelsus, a thousand-fold more worthy then his adversaries, and the immortall glory of Germany
items.note: The author's praise of Paracelsus over his adversaries.

items.quote: who had the absolute knowledge of all Divine and Humane sciences, beyond what will be believed of him
items.note: The author claims for Paracelsus absolute knowledge of all divine and human sciences.

items.quote: whom these men fear not to call a circumforaneous or rambling rayler, one that was no Phylosopher at all
items.name: Philerastian Physitians
items.note: What the opposing physicians call Paracelsus; reported to be rejected.

items.quote: with viperous hatred they accuse his course of life, aggravating his humane fraylties
items.note: The author grants Paracelsus human frailties and says his accusers make them heavier; he adds that all have failings.

items.quote: Lib. 1. cap. 19.
items.name: Galen
items.note: The margin note gives book and chapter beside Galen's reported words; it does not name the work.

items.quote: Whey, Butter and Cheese are the three first things of milk, for all Terresterity is Salt.
items.note: The note says what the three first things of milk are, and adds that all 'Terresterity' is Salt.

items.quote: I wish the ambitious Physitians of that time, who robbed others of their due praise, who cast a Serpents eye upon Theophrastus
items.note: The author blames the physicians of Paracelsus's time for envy toward him; the text uses the names Theophrastus and Paracelsus for the same man.

items.quote: who is the End of all Humane actions and Physick, viz. that we should love the Best and Greatest God, and all our neighbours as our selves
items.note: The text calls the giver of the command the End of all human actions and of Physick, and states the command.

items.quote: his human imperfections which none will excuse, they should have born with the like tendernes of compassion where with they pardon Galens impiety who scoffed at the doctrin of Moses & Christ
items.note: The author says none will excuse Paracelsus's imperfections, but they deserved the same forbearance given to Galen's impiety.

items.quote: Doubtles he would have more clearly have manifested to thankful posterity his Secrets which God disclosed to him, and written more plainly and perfectly of Preparations
items.note: The text says Paracelsus did not set out his Secrets clearly nor write plainly of Preparations, and lays this to the ill treatment he had.

items.quote: by being againe put to seek out the certainty and truth of that which Theophrastus discoursed and writ of, and to long for the true Preparations in the practicall proceeding
items.note: The present Spagyrick Profession is said to have to seek again the truth of what Theophrastus wrote and to lack the true Preparations in practice.

items.quote: there are so few to be found who have the true medicines prepared according to Theophrastus his minde, of which he treateth at large in his Books
items.note: Few have the true medicines prepared as Theophrastus meant, though his books treat of them at large.

items.quote: they require solutions, mortifications, cohibitions, resuscitations, &c. truly Phylosophycall, which cannot be understood without true Physick
items.note: Four kinds of working the true medicines require are named, without what is done to what; they cannot be understood without Physick, Astronomy and Chymistry.

items.quote: truly Phylosophycall
items.note: The named workings are qualified as 'truly Phylosophycall', which sets them apart from a plain sense of the same words; the lines given do not say how.

items.quote: nor are they compleated in a short time, but with much tediousnesse to Phylosophists who are impatient of delay
items.note: The preparations take long; those impatient of delay are called 'Phylosophists'.

items.quote: In his second Book of the difference of Pulses.
items.name: Galen
items.note: The margin note names the writing of Galen in which, by the passage, he scoffed at the doctrine of Moses and Christ.

items.quote: See Paracelsus in Paragr.
items.name: Paracelsus in Paragr.
items.note: The margin note names a writing of Paracelsus beside the statement that few have the true medicines.

items.quote: A Physitian must be an Astronomer, otherwise Paracelsus saith that his Physick is but imposture and a cheat.
items.name: Paracelsus
items.note: The note gives Paracelsus's saying that physick without astronomy is imposture.

items.quote: Therefore many with Icarus are drowned in a great Sea.
items.note: The note uses the figure of Icarus drowned for the many who fail.

items.quote: I think this wicked generation is not worthy of such medicines
items.note: The author's judgement that his generation is not worthy of the true medicines.

items.quote: his mighty and marvellous works from unworthy Men
items.note: God is said to with-hold his mighty works from unworthy men for the world's sins and ingratitude; a word of foreign script before these is unread.

items.quote: He will never suffer those Secrets to be known, especially in these corrupt and perilous times
items.note: The text says God will never let those Secrets be known, above all in these times.

items.quote: He will never suffer those Secrets to be known
items.note: Here the Secrets are never to be known; in CH3.46 the author hopes God will before long stir up some 'which may bring to light the Truth that is in sciences and Faculties'.

items.quote: almost all men have a burning desire after making Gold
items.note: The author says nearly all desire gold-making and (after the note mark) neglect the due preparation of their medicines.

items.quote: the onely cause thereof is their not knowing the Metaphysicks of Paracelsus, the true Phylosophy
items.note: The cause he gives: they do not know the Metaphysicks of Paracelsus, which he calls the true Phylosophy.

items.quote: those large Books which Theophrastus directeth unto in his Labyrinth of Physitians, before they set upon the preparations, separations and resolution of Naturall things
items.name: Theophrastus in his Labyrinth of Physitians
items.note: A writing of Theophrastus is named as directing to large books to be read first, before any preparation is begun.

items.quote: There are four Pillars of Physick, Phylosophy, Alchymistry, Astronomy, and the Physicall vertue or medicine.
items.note: The note numbers and names four Pillars of Physick.

items.quote: most Chymists betake themselves to Court, and are turned from the truth by the glitter of Court-service
items.note: The author observes that most Chymists go to court and are turned from the truth there.

items.quote: for many years I have taken notice that many have begun well, but deluded with these toyes, have made an ill end
items.note: He gives this as his own observation over many years.

items.quote: this Divine Spagyrie, the most wonderfull and approved Art
items.note: The art is named and set apart as divine and approved.

items.quote: though for many ages suspected of greatest uncertainty, and most abominable deceit
items.note: The author grants that the art has long been suspected of uncertainty and deceit, and says it is cast aside even by those who intend the same business.

items.quote: What is said of, or spoken against abuse, imposture, and wicked arts, is not that for which things otherwise good may or ought to be condemned
items.note: The abuse of a thing is no ground to condemn the thing; he adds that the better the thing, the worse its abuse.

items.quote: the Athenian Thrasos who will have Light to be Darkenesse, and Darkenesse to be Light
items.note: Opponents are named by a figure, 'the Athenian Thrasos'; the lines given do not say who is meant.

items.quote: the world seeketh not the Truth but its own Honour
items.note: The author's charge against the world that defends them.

items.quote: we our selves should be the cause of the imminent destruction of our own Kingdome
items.note: He says God gives 'us' up to hate one another and so to cause a near destruction of 'our own Kingdome'.

items.quote: O fountaine of Truth and Wisedome, consider our condition
items.note: The author turns to prayer at the close of the text given.

items.quote: that God would stirr up the minds of some which may bring to light the Truth that is in sciences and Faculties
items.note: He hopes God will soon move some to bring to light the truth in the sciences.

items.quote: for as yet the Invention of Arts hath not attained the utmost end
items.note: The author holds that the finding out of arts is not yet complete.

items.quote: confute the delusions and errours of the schoolmen not with words, but deeds; not Syllogistically, but Really and indeed
items.note: The schoolmen are to be refuted by deeds, not by words or syllogisms.

items.quote: the time of Revocation and Regeneration drawing nigh
items.what: the time of Revocation and Regeneration
items.note: A coming time is named, at which 'every imperfect thing will of necessity come to nought'.

items.quote: where Titles, Degrees and glistering Names make men proud, their is no humility, no life of Christ, no holy Spirit
items.note: Pride in titles and degrees is set against humility, the life of Christ and the holy Spirit.

items.quote: who suffer the Old man to be ruled by the Sydereall Spirit
items.note: Two names are used without explanation in the lines given: 'the Old man' and 'the Sydereall Spirit' that rules him in most.

items.quote: graciously deliver them from the chaines of Utter Darknesse and incessant janglings of Putatitious and conceited Schollers
items.note: The closing prayer for the lovers of Truth, against the wrangling of 'Putatitious' scholars.
